units: a mountain route is broken into sections sorted by the ground underfoot
the forest section follows wide switchbacks over soft ground
the gradient there stays moderate and steady
the scree zone comes from the rock face broken apart by frost
these stones shift underfoot and force quick footwork
the ridge section is swept by wind and pinches down in places
the descent leads to a damp gully where water-polished stone turns slick
each section calls for its own equipment
mapmakers flag these ground types with a graphic marking
this information lets a walker weigh the effort before setting out
text: Mapmakers break a mountain route into sections, and what sorts them is the ground underfoot. The first runs through forest: wide switchbacks, soil that gives a little, a climb that never steepens and never eases. Then the scree begins. Frost has been prying the rock face apart for years, and the loose stones it drops shift the moment you weight them, so you learn to step quick and light. Higher up, the route follows a ridge where the wind never lets go and the walking surface pinches down to a narrow lane. The last section drops into a damp gully, where running water has polished the stone until it turns slick. Each stretch asks for its own kit. On their maps the surveyors flag these surfaces with a shading of their own, so a walker can weigh what the day will cost before leaving the door.

units: the party set out from the shelter very early
a veil of mist still lay over the floor of the valley at the start
the guide had warned that the ford might be cut off if the snow melted fast
the descent to the water was made without a stop
the river was running fuller than the day before
the crossing was ordered from the lightest walkers upward
a rope was pulled taut between two boulders to secure the passage
the packs were carried over apart from the heaviest walkers
the party then dried off in an open clearing in the forest
the guide saw the whole maneuver as an ordinary precaution
text: They left the stone shelter before the light came, while mist still lay thick along the floor of the valley. The guide had said it plainly the night before: if the thaw picked up, the ford would be gone by midday. So they went down to the water without stopping once, and reached it as the gray began to lift. The river ran fuller than it had the day before, rolling stones along its bed with a low knock. The guide sent the lightest across first and worked up by weight, a rope pulled taut between two boulders. The packs went over on their own, apart from the heaviest walkers. On the far bank a clearing gave them dry ground, and they wrung out their clothes there. Back home the same walkers told it with a quiet sort of pride. The guide only shrugged. To him it had been an ordinary bit of care.

units: you must read the angle of the slope before committing to a mountain flank
the steepness is what decides the danger
a gentle grade holds its snow in place
a sharp grade lets the snow go the moment you walk on it
a pole serves to test how the snow layers are stacked
a top layer sliding over a hardened layer means you turn back
it is better to travel along a rib of ground than in a hollow of the relief
a chute gathers moving snow and multiplies its force
walkers have to cross one at a time so that they are not swept away together
the sound of water under the snow reveals a void beneath the feet
text: Before you commit to a steep flank, read the angle of the slope. Steepness is what decides the danger. A gentle grade holds its snow in place; a sharp one lets go the moment your boot lands, and what lets go carries the walker down with it. Push a pole into the snowpack and feel how it is stacked. If the top layer slides over a hard crust below, turn back, because that pairing is a break waiting to happen. Pick a line along a rib rather than a hollow, since a hollow funnels everything that moves and multiplies its force. Send the party across one walker at a time, so that a single slip cannot take the whole rope. And listen for water running under your feet: that hollow rush means an empty vault below, and an empty vault gives way under load. If doubt is left, go down. Turning back costs you nothing but the walk.

units: the coast path has been losing ground for two seasons
salt spray and swell hollow out the cliff from underneath
walkers keep using the passage all the same
the warning board keeps disappearing under the greenery
the woman in charge of the paths admits that banning has failed
a new line has been pegged out farther back from the sea in the low heath
that line has cut steps and a timber handrail
walkers take it because it is pleasanter, not out of obedience
the old passage is closing itself under the thorn scrub
the woman in charge holds that a better offer beats a telling off
text: Two seasons now, the coast path has been giving way, chewed at by spray and by swell that hollows the cliff from underneath. Walkers keep on using the path all the same. The view is worth it, the going is easy, and the warning board disappears under greenery about as fast as anyone can clear it. The woman who looks after the paths says so without fuss: banning people did not work, they tried it. So they tried something else. A fallback line was pegged out farther back, through the low heath, with cut steps and a timber handrail. People take it because it is pleasanter, not because they were told to. The threatened stretch is quietly closing itself under thorn scrub. Scolding walkers buys you nothing, she says with a shrug of the shoulders. Giving them something better buys you the path.

units: two valleys on either flank of the same range have almost nothing in common
the eastern valley is broad and flat
its river loops back in slow bends and carries silt
grazing land runs down there to the edge of the water
the western valley is a narrow notch
a fast stream drops through it from pool to pool and throws up foam
its sides carry scattered trees hanging off the rock
the difference comes down to the gradient
ground that barely tilts lets the river wander
the first valley is walked without effort while the second is climbed
text: Two valleys lie on opposite flanks of one range, and they have almost nothing in common. The eastern one opens wide and flat. Its river loops back on itself in slow bends, brown with silt, moving so quietly you hear nothing, and grazing land runs all the way down to the bank. The western one is a narrow notch cut deep into rock. A stream drops through it from pool to pool, white with foam, and thin stands of trees hang off the sides wherever a root can grip. The whole difference comes down to gradient. Where the ground barely tilts, the water takes its time and builds its bends; where it plunges, the water runs straight and digs. Walkers feel that in their legs. The first valley you stroll through. The second you climb like a staircase. Two neighbors, two ways of wearing down the rock.

units: the writer calls up the feeling that comes before a ridge line half hidden in mist
he blames travel as it is sold for running like a checklist
he puts forward three ways of giving up a fixed program
the first is to move very slowly
stopping when the shade settles in belongs to that first way
the second is to walk the same trail at another time of year
that return reveals that the colors, the sounds and the smells have changed
the third is to leave the names of the summits deliberately unlearned
the writer refuses to treat a landscape as something one collects
he sets the walker willing to dawdle against the one who comes to take inventory
text: Stand in front of a ridge half swallowed by mist and something in you goes looking for more than a picture. Everyone has felt it. Travel as it is sold to us runs on lists instead: a lookout, a lake, a photogenic clearing, tick, tick, tick. Let me argue for three ways of losing your route. The first is slowness. Walk at the pace of a grazing herd, and stop wherever the shade settles in. The second is return. Come back to the same trail in the opposite season and find that its colors, its noises and its smells have all changed hands. The third is chosen ignorance. Do not learn the names of the summits beforehand; let them stand there as shapes. A landscape is not a thing to collect. It opens to whoever will lose an afternoon in it, and it shuts against whoever arrives to take inventory.

units: the path repair worker started out hauling stone for the man before him
his first jobs were all muscle
he had to clear away the rubble that came down onto the track
he bedded wooden drainage bars across the slope
he was later handed the setting of the route markers
a marker set wrong can send a walker straight off a drop
he was trained to lay stone without mortar
he raised a first retaining wall under someone else's eye
he now lays out the routes himself, working out the workable gradient and where the water goes
he teaches his apprentices that a well-drained path mends itself
text: The man who keeps the paths in repair learned the work by hauling stone for the fellow who held the job before him. The early years were all muscle: shoveling away the rubble that came down onto the track, bedding wooden drain bars across the slope, scraping out the runnels. Marking the route came later, and it weighed more, because a sign set wrong can walk somebody straight off a drop. He was trained to lay stone without mortar, and he raised his first retaining wall with an older hand watching every course. These days he lays out the lines himself. He works out how much gradient a path can take, angles it so water leaves rather than follows, and picks where the footing goes. He trains apprentices now. His first lesson fits in one line: drain a path properly and it mends itself.

units: the book deals with high mountain paths and it wins the reader over
what it is worth comes from a working method the author owns up to
the author walked every route in it himself
he walked them at different times of the year
the timings he gives can therefore be trusted
first-hand experience brings out dangers that no map carries
the book flags in particular a seeping rock, a ford swollen after rain, and a scree slope that turns loose in a thaw
the reader comes away better equipped and warier
the photographs are faulted for showing nothing but clear sky
that visual choice makes the route look kinder than it is
text: This book about high mountain paths wins you over, and it wins you over because of how it was made. The author walked every route in it himself, and walked them across the seasons rather than once in fine weather. That is why the timings hold up. It is also why the warnings do: no survey on paper tells you where the rock seeps, where the ford swells after a storm, where a scree slope starts shedding as soon as the thaw sets in. The result is a reader who arrives better equipped, and who arrives warier. The pictures are another matter. Every one of them was taken under an open sky, so the mist that governs half of these outings never shows up at all. That weakens the case, since it makes the walking look kinder than it is. The book teaches well. It comforts a little too quickly.

units: the writer doubts that his earlier message ever went out
the letter box in the village looked as though nobody had emptied it
he is writing from an inn down in a valley
his stay has run on longer than he had meant
his boots gave out on the third pass
the vehicle meant to carry him back does not run outside the busy months
he first thought he would have to give up the trip
the innkeeper found him a driver who takes goods over to the next town
a tradesman resoled his boots for next to nothing
he announces that he leaves two stages earlier than planned
text: I hope my last card actually reached you. The box in the village looked as though nobody had emptied it since the spring. I am writing from an inn down in the valley, where I have stayed on far longer than I meant to. Two things went wrong at once: my boots gave out on the third pass, and the little bus that was supposed to carry me back does not run outside the busy months. For a day I thought I would have to give up and find my own way home. Then the innkeeper had an idea. Her brother drives crates over to the next town every week, and he is glad to take me along. Meanwhile a cobbler has resoled my boots for next to nothing at all. So I set off the day after tomorrow, two stages shorter and one story richer. Write to the return address; I will collect the post when I get there.

units: the number of visitors swings sharply from one time of year to another
the gap does not fall where people picture it
in the warm months the visitors pour in
they stay bunched on a very small handful of waymarked routes
they hardly walk and they photograph endlessly
in the cold months the visitors are few but they spread out off the paths
it is those scattered visitors who do the most harm
ground packed down by a crowd recovers
one walker cutting across a forest clearing upsets the birds that are nesting
the warden would rather open new routes and put up boards that explain than hand out penalties
text: Does the number of visitors change with the season? Hugely, says the forest warden, but not in the way people picture. In the warm months they pour in, she says, and they stay bunched on three or four waymarked routes; they hardly walk at all and they photograph everything. In the cold months almost nobody comes, yet the few who do go wherever they like, paths or no paths. And which of them causes trouble? The second lot, no question. A crowd on a trail packs the soil down, and soil recovers from that. One walker cutting across a clearing puts the nesting birds off, and that does not come back. So what do you do about it? She would rather widen the choice: fresh routes opened in the quiet months, boards that tell you about the nests instead of forbidding you. Does it work? Better than fines, she says, laughing.
